{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-al-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"c25231c9ec6437d3fe4d9972a665093beaaa405f14af05481a5a65e30c12133d","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-al-class-d:lineage:28","source_registry_sha256":"ea8231e949706ecda9f2a398d6eaf9ab30e224ac7defb0e6291b764b84ed0d95","source_liveness_sha256":"e524456f547beacfeca0647b02ef401523e58aa5b835501e7cbdd821b6546315"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings","heading":"C — Drugs, following distance, stopping distance and crashes","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Drugs, following distance, stopping distance and crashes

FACT_ID: sec07-F01 | anchor: A37
Many drugs can weaken your ability to drive safely, whether a doctor prescribed them or you bought them over the counter. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F02 | anchor: A37
When you take prescription medicine, ask your doctor about any side effects that could affect your driving. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F03 | anchor: A37
Some non-prescription allergy remedies and cold pills contain codeine, alcohol, antihistamines or bromides, and each of these can affect driving. [A37]
Why it matters: a remedy bought without a prescription is not automatically safe to drive on.
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F04 | anchor: A37
Antihistamines, taken for cold congestion and allergies, can cause inattention, confusion and drowsiness, and some are even used as sleep aids. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F05 | anchor: A37
Barbiturates are sedatives used mainly for sleep, and overusing them brings drowsiness, confusion and poor coordination much like drunkenness, leaving the person unfit to drive. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F06 | anchor: A37
The most dangerous drugs, such as LSD and heroin, are available only illegally and can leave users unaware of their surroundings, so no one under their influence may drive. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F07 | anchor: A37
Studies cited in the manual link marijuana use to more traffic-violation arrests, and experts agree it should not be used when driving. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F08 | anchor: A37
Combining alcohol with drugs does not merely double the effect; it multiplies it and has caused deaths, so never drink while taking medicine. [A37]
Why it matters: the common belief that a drink only doubles a pill's effect is exactly what the manual calls wrong.
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F09 | anchor: A37
For a chronic illness or physical impairment, the physician is responsible for telling the patient about any driving limits that may apply. [A37]
Source: [A37 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec07-F10 | anchor: A38
Following too closely causes most rear-end collisions, and the space ahead of your car, called following distance, is the space you can control most easily. [A38]
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F11 | anchor: A38
Set your following distance by the speed of traffic and the condition of the road, leaving enough room to stop if you must. [A38]
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F12 | anchor: A38
The old rule of one car length for every ten miles per hour has given way to the two-second rule, which the manual calls easier to apply and safer. [A38]
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F13 | anchor: A38
For the two-second rule, pick a fixed object ahead, start counting one thousand one, one thousand two as the car ahead passes it, and if you reach it first, ease off until the gap is safe. [A38]
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F14 | anchor: A38
When road or weather conditions are poor, stretch the gap to a four- or five-second count, and use the longer gap too when driving a vehicle longer than a car. [A38]
Why it matters: two seconds is the minimum in good conditions, not the answer for rain or long vehicles.
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F15 | anchor: A38
Watch for brake lights and a shrinking gap ahead, and move your foot to the brake pedal right away so you are ready to stop. [A38]
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F16 | anchor: A38
How far your car needs to stop helps decide a safe speed, and actual stopping distance depends first on the driver's mental and physical reaction time. [A38]
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F17 | anchor: A38
Pavement type and condition change stopping distance a great deal, since rough dry concrete grips far better than slippery brick or smooth asphalt. [A38]
Source: [A38 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0038]

FACT_ID: sec07-F18 | anchor: A39
Tire type, condition and tread depth all determine how much traction you have for stopping, so check the owner's manual or a dealer for the right tire size. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F19 | anchor: A39
Large, wide tires may stop sooner on smooth dry roads but skid or hydroplane more easily when wet, while small, narrow tires may cut through standing water yet lose overall stopping power. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F20 | anchor: A39
Chassis design, weight distribution, suspension, shock absorbers and the type, condition and balance of the brakes all affect stopping, and a brake that locks before the others can cause serious trouble. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F21 | anchor: A39
Wind direction and speed matter too, because a strong tail wind can lengthen a sudden stop at high speed more than drivers expect. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F22 | anchor: A39
The manual's stopping-distance chart gives 27 feet of thinking distance plus 34.7 feet of braking distance, or 61.7 feet in total, at 25 MPH. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F23 | anchor: A39
On the same chart, at 55 MPH a driver covers 60 feet while reacting and 168 feet while braking, 228 feet in all. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F24 | anchor: A39
At 65 MPH the chart shows 71 feet of thinking distance and 234.7 feet of braking distance, a total of 305.7 feet. [A39]
Why it matters: braking distance grows much faster than thinking distance as speed rises.
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F25 | anchor: A39
If you are in a crash you must stop at once and help anyone injured, call for medical help if needed, and warn other traffic with flags, flares or whatever you have before police arrive. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F26 | anchor: A39
Do not move injured people unless it is absolutely necessary to get them away from fire or another danger, and keep them lying or sitting down until trained medical help arrives. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F27 | anchor: A39
Give first aid, keep the injured comfortable and treat for shock, but remember a layman can give too much first aid; a Red Cross or similar course is recommended. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F28 | anchor: A39
In any type of crash you must stop, tell the others involved your name, address and registration number, and let them see your driver license. [A39]
Source: [A39 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec07-F29 | anchor: A40
A crash with injury or death must be reported by the fastest means available, to local police inside a city or town or to the State Troopers on a state highway. [A40]
Source: [A40 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F30 | anchor: A40
After a crash with injury, death or $500 or more in damage, the involved driver has 30 days to send a written Form SR-31 if the at-fault party was uninsured; when both parties were insured, neither files it. [A40]
Source: [A40 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec07-F31 | anchor: A40
SR-31 forms go to the ALEA Safety Responsibility Unit by mail or can be submitted online through ALEA's driver license website. [A40]
Source: [A40 -> src:rdmv-al-d:alabama-law-enforcement-agency-alea-driv:handbook:pdf-0040]

Glossary: following distance — the space cushion between your car and the vehicle ahead [A38]. Thinking distance — how far the car travels while the driver reacts; braking distance — how far it travels once the brakes take hold [A39]. Barbiturate — a sedative drug used mainly for sleep [A37].
Memory aid: two seconds in good weather, four or five when it is bad [A38].
